Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions), Marcus Reed (CTO - Helios), Anika Zhou (Cloud Architect), Luis Fernandez (Security), Tanya Park (Product)

topics: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway architecture
Regional model hosting and data residency
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we've got a full house. Quick intro round?
[00:10] Marcus: Marcus Reed here, CTO at Helios DataWorks. We're re-evaluating our LLM infra and network constraints are the blocker.
[00:18] Jordan: Great, Marcus. Priya?
[00:20] Priya: Priya Nair, Redwood SE. I'll drive the technical bits. Samir's on for solutions questions.
[00:25] Samir: Hi all.
[00:27] Anika: Anika — cloud architect, handling VPC design. We're primarily on AWS but have a few GCP projects.
[00:32] Luis: Luis from security, will focus on compliance and egress.
[00:35] Jordan: Cool. High level — Helios wants to run models in a private deployment to keep data inside our VPC, low egress, and have auditability, correct? Marcus: correct.
[00:45] Marcus: Yep. We have two constraints: (1) data residency — models and inference must run in us-east-1 for now due to client contracts; (2) outgoing egress must be tightly controlled, ideally no public internet access from the model hosts.
[00:58] Priya: Understood. We typically support three private connectivity patterns: VPC peering to Redwood Dedicated hosts, Transit Gateway for multi-VPC scale, or PrivateLink / private endpoints where supported. Each has tradeoffs for IP management and cross-account routing.
[01:15] Anika: Can you run us through latency and routing differences? We need sub-50ms p95 for our main inference path.
[01:23] Priya: Sure. In-region Dedicated nodes hosted in your VPC via private endpoints will give the best latency; peering can be equivalent if it's cross-account but in-region, typically sub-40-60ms depending on AZ placement and path. Transit Gateway helps when you have many spoke VPCs — it centralizes routing but adds a small hop, usually a few ms. PrivateLink avoids route table complexity but requires AWS NLB and ENI behavior — it's generally stable for TCP TLS workloads.
[01:50] Luis: How do you handle egress — like if the model needs to download a tokenizer or call external telemetry? We need to avoid accidental public egress.
[02:00] Priya: We recommend using VPC endpoints for S3 and other AWS services; for third-party telemetry we can configure egress-only NAT or a customer-managed proxy. Redwood's Private control plane can be configured to only talk to your VPC via PrivateLink so control-plane traffic never goes over public internet if you choose that. Note — some model pulling during onboarding may need temporary access; we can preload model artifacts into an S3 bucket you own.
[02:30] Marcus: Who owns the IP ranges? We want to avoid overlapping CIDRs with existing infra.
[02:35] Samir: Good question. For peering we require non-overlapping CIDRs. With Transit Gateway you can do route propagation to avoid conflicts but still non-overlapping is simplest. With PrivateLink the interface ENIs live in your subnets and we don't need wide peering — that can help with overlap.
[02:52] Anika: What about cross-region fallback? We have customers in eu-west but legal requires primary in us-east. If us-east has capacity issues, can you failover to say us-west with encryption and still meet data residency?
[03:05] Priya: For strict data residency you'd want to avoid cross-region failover for protected data. We support routing policies to prefer in-region and can fail open to another region only for non-sensitive workloads. For Helios' case we can pin the model version to us-east for Protected tag, and have a fallback only for non-production tiers.
[03:25] Luis: Audit logs — we need per-request logging and key access logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:30] Jordan: That's part of Redwood Console: token-level cost and latency breakdowns, plus per-request traces. For Private deployments we can push logs to your Kinesis/CloudWatch/S3. We also support customer-managed KMS so key access is auditable.
[03:46] Anika: Network specifics — what ports and ranges do we need to open?
[03:50] Priya: At a minimum we use HTTPS/TLS 443 for model inference APIs. For control plane there might be additional ports for health checks but standard is 443. We'll provide a concrete sg/route table template. If you choose PrivateLink, you'll have ENIs in subnets and security groups applied there.
[04:05] Marcus: Have you done Transit Gateway designs with strict egress and inspection? We run an IDS in our TGW central firewall.
[04:12] Samir: Yes — TGW pairs well with inspection. We'll publish the subnets the Redwood endpoints will live in; you can route through the inspection VPC. The caveat is ensuring route priority so model traffic doesn't hairpin or add unexpected costs.
[04:28] Luis: Encryption in transit — do you support mTLS between our services and the model endpoints?
[04:33] Priya: We terminate TLS at the service by default but can support mutual TLS if you manage certs or use a proxy that enforces client certs. For PrivateLink the interface endpoints will accept TLS connections, and we can require client-cert verification in front of the runtime.
[04:48] Anika: What's the onboarding timeline for a Dedicated pilot? We want a small pilot in two weeks.
[04:52] Jordan: Typical pilot for Dedicated in-region is 2–3 weeks assuming network rules are provided. Week 0: runbook + IPs; Week 1: provisioning and sample model; Week 2: bench and tuning. We can compress if you provide network details early.
[05:08] Marcus: Ok. Security questionnaire — we'll need SOC2 evidence and encryption docs.
[05:12] Jordan: We'll share the security pack. Also can provide a live session with our security engineer.
[05:18] Anika: Are there any gotchas with SNI or hostnames? We do SNI-based routing in our NLBs.
[05:22] Priya: SNI is fine; for PrivateLink the hostnames can be customized in DNS. If you use peering you'd resolve the private hostnames to peered IPs. Sometimes leakage occurs if public DNS is still pointing to a public endpoint — we recommend split-horizon DNS during cutover.
[05:40] Luis: For egress monitoring, can Redwood tag requests with tenant IDs? We need to link logs back to customer request IDs.
[05:46] Jordan: Yes — request metadata includes tenant and api-key token ids. We can include tissue-level? (laughter) — sorry, I mean token-level.
[05:55] Marcus: (laughs) we saw that in another transcript where a word got swapped.
[05:58] Priya: Another practical: model KV cache — does that store any customer PII? For us it's ephemeral key-value cache; we can keep it in-memory and never persist to disk for sensitive workloads.
[06:12] Anika: If we use PrivateLink in us-east, do we need to open any public egress for health checks?
[06:18] Priya: No, health checks can be internal. The only times we reach out to public is for support debug snapshots if you opt in. We default to internal-only.
[06:27] Marcus: Pricing question briefly — is Dedicated billed by reserved capacity plus egress?
[06:32] Jordan: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools (monthly/annual) with predictable throughput. Egress is customer network egress — Redwood charges for hosted egress only; for Private deployments egress is part of your cloud costs. We'll include a pricing sketch in follow-up.
[06:45] Anika: For the pilot, what info do you need from us now?
[06:48] Priya: We'll need: (1) CIDR ranges for the VPC(s) and the subnets you want endpoints in, (2) preferred connectivity pattern (peering, TGW, PrivateLink), (3) security group baselines, (4) KMS key ARNs if you want customer-managed keys, (5) telemetry/endpoint where logs should be forwarded.
[07:05] Marcus: We'll share that by tomorrow.
[07:07] Jordan: Great — we'll also send the network runbook and an architecture diagram template.
[07:12] Tanya: Quick note — compliance team needs data access review — can Redwood restrict query outputs or redact?
[07:18] Priya: We can instrument request/response filtering at the proxy layer and support output redaction for certain sensitive tokens; that's usually done in the app layer but we have hooks. We'll document options.
[07:30] Anika: One edge case — we have a legacy VPC with overlapping 10.0/8 ranges in some teams. PrivateLink seems appealing. Any limitations on concurrent endpoints?
[07:38] Priya: No hard limits from Redwood, but AWS ENI quotas apply. We'll coordinate recommended subnet size and ENI counts.
[07:48] Marcus: Ok let's go over next steps quickly.
[07:50] Jordan: Next steps: send runbook (Jordan), provision bench tenant (Priya/Samir), Helios to send CIDRs and KMS ARNs (Anika/Marcus). We schedule bench for next Tue if possible.
[08:02] Marcus: Sounds good.
[08:05] Luis: One last security ask — can logs be redacted before they hit our SIEM? We don't want raw PII in logs.
[08:11] Priya: Yes, we can provide redaction pipelines and documented patterns for the built-in audit export. We'll include examples.
[08:20] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts and a calendar invite for the bench.
[08:25] Marcus: Thanks all.
[08:28] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-transcriptions present (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache). Some speaker labels normalized to names and a generic "Speaker 2" present from the auto-capture.
